meta.titre: Wave-Particle Duality: Photons, Work Function and de Broglie Waves
meta.sous_theme: photoelectric effect and de Broglie waves

sections.contenu_markdown: When the sun hits the solar panels that now power clinics in the villages around Bamenda, light is not just warming the metal: it is knocking electrons loose one at a time. That simple fact, and the matching discovery that electrons spread out and diffract like waves, forced physicists in the early twentieth century to abandon the idea that everything is either a wave or a particle. The GCE Advanced Level paper returns to this theme every year, asking which observations a wave theory can explain and which need photons, and asking you to use $E = hf$ and $\lambda = h/p$ with confidence.

items: Electromagnetic waves obey $c = f\lambda$ in a vacuum, with $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Interference and diffraction are properties of waves.
Kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ and momentum is $p = mv$.
One electronvolt is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of $1\ \mathrm{V}$, so $1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

sections.titre: Photons, work function and de Broglie wavelength
sections.contenu_markdown:
**The photoelectric effect** is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of high enough frequency falls on it. Experiments show that:

1. below a **threshold frequency** $f_0$, which depends on the metal, no electrons are emitted however intense the radiation;
2. above $f_0$, emission begins at once, with no measurable delay, even for very dim light;
3. the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons increases with frequency and does **not** depend on intensity;
4. the number of electrons emitted per second (the photocurrent) is proportional to intensity.

Classical wave theory expects energy to build up steadily in the surface, so emission at any frequency if the light is intense enough or the exposure long enough, a delay for dim light, and a maximum kinetic energy that grows with intensity. Only observation 4 agrees with it. This is why the effect is evidence for the **particle nature** of radiation.

**Einstein's model.** Radiation arrives in packets called photons, each of energy $E = hf = hc/\lambda$. One photon gives all of its energy to one electron. The **work function** $\phi$ is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface, so $\phi = hf_0$. Conservation of energy gives
$$hf = \phi + E_{k,\max}$$
and the **stopping potential** $V_s$, which just stops the fastest electrons, satisfies $eV_s = E_{k,\max}$.

**de Broglie's hypothesis.** A particle of momentum $p$ has an associated wavelength
$$\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}$$
A photon has momentum $p = h/\lambda = E/c$. Electron diffraction by a thin crystal or graphite film gives rings, as waves would, and so shows the **wave nature** of electrons. For an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference $V$, $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = eV$, so $p = \sqrt{2meV}$.

Interference (Young's double slit) and diffraction of light are evidence of the **wave nature** of electromagnetic radiation; the photoelectric effect is evidence of its **particle nature**. Both descriptions are needed: this is wave-particle duality.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When data of maximum kinetic energy or stopping potential against frequency are given or a graph is described.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Rewrite the equation as $E_{k,\max} = hf - \phi$ or $V_s = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{\phi}{e}$. A graph of $E_{k,\max}$ against $f$ is a straight line with gradient $h$, an intercept on the frequency axis equal to $f_0$ and an intercept on the energy axis equal to $-\phi$. A graph of $V_s$ against $f$ has gradient $h/e$. Changing the metal shifts the line sideways but leaves the gradient the same; changing the intensity changes nothing on this graph.

variantes.nom: de Broglie wavelength and electron diffraction
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a particle's wavelength is asked for, or diffraction of electrons or neutrons is discussed.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Find the momentum first, then divide it into $h$. For a charged particle accelerated through $V$, use $p=\sqrt{2mqV}$. Appreciable diffraction needs a wavelength comparable to the spacing of the atoms, about $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, which is why electrons of a few tens of electronvolts are used with crystals. A moving cricket ball has a wavelength far too small to detect, so its wave behaviour is never seen.

variantes.nom: Wave or particle: which evidence supports which
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked which observation shows the wave nature or the particle nature of radiation or matter.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Observation | Shows |
|---|---|
| Interference and diffraction of light | wave nature of radiation |
| Polarisation of light | transverse wave nature of radiation |
| Threshold frequency, no delay, $E_{k,\max}$ independent of intensity | particle nature of radiation |
| Electron diffraction by crystals | wave nature of electrons |
| Electrons deflected as single charges in a magnetic field | particle nature of electrons |

sections.enonce_markdown: Light of wavelength $450\ \mathrm{nm}$ falls on a metal surface whose work function is $2.30\ \mathrm{eV}$. Use $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $e = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ and $m_e = 9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$. Calculate (a) the energy of one photon, in joules and in electronvolts, (b) the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, (c) the stopping potential, and (d) the longest wavelength that can cause emission.

etapes.justification: The energy of a photon is fixed by the wavelength of the light through $E=hc/\lambda$.

etapes.action: Convert the work function to joules.
etapes.justification: The photon energy and the work function must be in the same unit before they are subtracted.

etapes.action: Apply Einstein's equation to find the maximum kinetic energy.
etapes.justification: One photon gives all of its energy to one electron, so what is left after paying the work function is kinetic energy.
The stopping potential does work $eV_s$ equal to the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons.
At the threshold the photon energy equals the work function exactly, so the electrons leave with no kinetic energy; any longer wavelength carries less energy.

sections.conclusion_markdown: A photon of this light carries $2.76\ \mathrm{eV}$, which exceeds the work function of $2.30\ \mathrm{eV}$, so electrons are emitted with a maximum kinetic energy of $7.40\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}$ and a stopping potential of $0.463\ \mathrm{V}$. The longest wavelength that works is about $540\ \mathrm{nm}$; the $450\ \mathrm{nm}$ light is shorter, as it must be.

items.erreur_markdown: If I increase the intensity of the light, the photoelectrons leave with more kinetic energy.
items.pourquoi_faux: Increasing intensity means more photons per second, not more energy per photon. Each electron still absorbs one photon.
items.correction_markdown: Intensity changes the **number** of electrons emitted per second (the photocurrent). The maximum kinetic energy depends only on the frequency and the metal.

items.erreur_markdown: Any light will release electrons if it is bright enough or shone on the metal for long enough.
items.pourquoi_faux: This is the classical prediction, and experiment contradicts it. A single photon below the threshold frequency does not have enough energy and photons do not add their energies.
items.correction_markdown: No emission occurs below $f_0$, however intense the light or long the exposure.

items.erreur_markdown: The energy of a photon of wavelength $\lambda$ is $E = hc\lambda$.
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength. A shorter wavelength means a higher frequency and a larger energy.
items.correction_markdown: $E=hf=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, and the wavelength must be in metres: $450\ \mathrm{nm}=450\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}$.

items.erreur_markdown: The photoelectric effect proves that light is a stream of particles, so light is not a wave.
items.pourquoi_faux: Interference and diffraction of light can only be explained by waves. One model alone cannot account for all observations.
items.correction_markdown: Light shows wave behaviour in propagation (interference, diffraction) and particle behaviour in its interaction with matter (photoelectric effect). This is duality.

items.erreur_markdown: Only light has a wavelength; a moving electron or a moving ball does not.
items.pourquoi_faux: The relation $\lambda=h/p$ applies to every moving particle.
items.correction_markdown: Electrons diffract, so their wavelength is observable. A ball has a wavelength too, but because $p$ is so large $\lambda$ is far too small to show any effect.

items.enonce_markdown: Radiation of frequency $8.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is incident on a metal of work function $3.0\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$. Take $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$ and $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (a) Calculate the energy of a photon of the radiation. (b) Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons. (c) Find the threshold frequency and the threshold wavelength. (d) State, with a reason, what happens to the photocurrent and to the maximum kinetic energy when the intensity is doubled.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Photon energy: $E=hf=6.63\times10^{-34}\times8.0\times10^{14}=5.30\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$. Since this exceeds $\phi=3.0\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$, electrons are emitted.

(b) $E_{k,\max}=E-\phi=5.30\times10^{-19}-3.0\times10^{-19}=2.30\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

(c) $f_0=\dfrac{\phi}{h}=\dfrac{3.0\times10^{-19}}{6.63\times10^{-34}}=4.52\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $\lambda_0=\dfrac{c}{f_0}=\dfrac{3.00\times10^{8}}{4.52\times10^{14}}=6.63\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

(d) Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons arriving per second, so the photocurrent doubles. Each photon is unchanged, so $E_{k,\max}$ stays the same.

**$E=5.30\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$; $E_{k,\max}=2.30\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$; $f_0=4.52\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $\lambda_0=6.63\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$; the photocurrent doubles and $E_{k,\max}$ is unchanged.**

items.enonce_markdown: In an experiment on a metal surface the stopping potential is $0.30\ \mathrm{V}$ for light of frequency $6.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $1.54\ \mathrm{V}$ for light of frequency $9.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Take $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. (a) Calculate the gradient of the graph of stopping potential against frequency. (b) Hence find a value for the Planck constant. (c) Calculate the work function of the metal in joules and in electronvolts. (d) Find the threshold frequency.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $V_s=\dfrac{h}{e}f-\dfrac{\phi}{e}$, so the gradient is $\dfrac{h}{e}$. Gradient $=\dfrac{1.54-0.30}{9.0\times10^{14}-6.0\times10^{14}}=4.13\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{V\,s}$.

(b) $h=e\times\text{gradient}=1.60\times10^{-19}\times4.13\times10^{-15}=6.61\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$.

(c) At the first point $eV_s=hf-\phi$, so $\phi=hf-eV_s=6.61\times10^{-34}\times6.0\times10^{14}-1.60\times10^{-19}\times0.30=3.49\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$, which is 2.18 eV.

(d) $f_0=\dfrac{\phi}{h}=\dfrac{3.49\times10^{-19}}{6.61\times10^{-34}}=5.27\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

**$h=6.61\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$; $\phi=3.49\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$ ($2.18\ \mathrm{eV}$); $f_0=5.27\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$.**

items.enonce_markdown: A photon and an electron each have a wavelength of $0.20\ \mathrm{nm}$, comparable with the spacing of atoms in a crystal. Take $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$, $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. (a) Calculate the photon energy in electronvolts. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy of the electron in electronvolts. (c) Find the potential difference through which the electron must be accelerated from rest to have this wavelength. (d) Compare the two energies and explain why they differ although the wavelengths are equal.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Photon energy: $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{0.20\times10^{-9}}=9.94\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{J}=6220\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(b) Electron momentum: $p=\dfrac{h}{\lambda}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{0.20\times10^{-9}}=3.32\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Kinetic energy: $E_k=\dfrac{p^{2}}{2m_e}=\dfrac{(3.32\times10^{-24})^{2}}{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}}=6.03\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}=37.7\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(c) The electron needs $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}=eV$, so $V=E_k/e=37.7\ \mathrm{V}$.

(d) $\dfrac{E_{photon}}{E_{k}}=\dfrac{9.94\times10^{-16}}{6.03\times10^{-18}}=165$. A photon of this wavelength carries about 165 times more energy than the electron of the same wavelength, because the photon has $E=pc$ whereas the electron has $E_k=p^{2}/2m_e$, so the ratio is $2m_ec/p$, which is large at this momentum. The two have the same momentum $p=h/\lambda$.

**$E_{photon}=6220\ \mathrm{eV}$; electron $E_k=37.7\ \mathrm{eV}$ after acceleration through $37.7\ \mathrm{V}$; the photon has about 165 times more energy.**

items_markdown: Photoelectric observations that wave theory cannot explain are the threshold frequency, the lack of delay, and the independence of the maximum kinetic energy from intensity; the photocurrent proportional to intensity is the only one it can explain.
Photon energy is $E=hf=hc/\lambda$; Einstein's equation is $hf=\phi+E_{k,\max}$ with $\phi=hf_0$ and $eV_s=E_{k,\max}$.
A graph of $E_{k,\max}$ (or $eV_s$) against $f$ is a straight line of gradient $h$ (or $h/e$ for $V_s$); it meets the frequency axis at $f_0$.
The de Broglie wavelength of any moving particle is $\lambda=h/p$; a photon has momentum $p=h/\lambda=E/c$.
Interference and diffraction show the wave nature of radiation; the photoelectric effect shows its particle nature; electron diffraction shows the wave nature of matter.
